summary:
Sol Horizon: Outpost Commander is a 3D browser game where students run a lunar or Martian outpost for 10 sols (days). Players balance power, oxygen, food and radiation shielding, repair equipment by hand, drive a rover to recover supplies, and shelter from solar flares, so young learners feel the engineering trade-offs that decide whether a mission succeeds.

The problem: Space STEM content often oversimplifies mission engineering or makes it too complex for young learners.

Our solution: A first and third person survival game on the Moon or Mars. Solar power runs the oxygen recycler and greenhouse, and the radiation shield protects the crew. All four systems wear down and need hands-on repair. Players face a lunar night, a Martian dust storm and solar flares, and must plan ahead.

How it plays: Walk or drive a rover across dunes, craters and rocks. Complete three tasks each sol. When a flare warning sounds, enter the habitat through its airlock to cut radiation. Adventure mode is forgiving; Survival mode is hard.

What players learn: why power storage matters at night, why shielding must be built before a flare, and why every system depends on the others.

Built with Three.js, it runs in any modern browser. Gravity, day length and radiation values are simplified and inspired by NASA mission information.
details:
Sol Horizon: Outpost Commander is a 3D browser game in which students run a lunar or Martian outpost for 10 sols (days). Players walk in first or third person, or drive a rover, to repair solar arrays, an oxygen recycler, a greenhouse and a radiation shield. Power runs life support and food production, so a lunar night or Martian dust storm forces players to plan ahead. Solar flares require running into the habitat’s shelter. Each sol has three tasks, and Adventure and Survival modes set how forgiving the game is.

Benefits: The game teaches systems thinking through play. Players see that every system depends on the others and that trade-offs have consequences. It runs in any modern browser with no download, so schools with limited hardware can use it.

Intended impact: To help young learners understand the engineering trade-offs behind real missions, and to make space STEM concepts hands-on and memorable.

Tools: JavaScript, HTML and CSS, Three.js for 3D graphics, and a Google Font for text. We developed it with the help of an AI assistant (Claude).

Creativity: The outpost, rover and terrain are generated in code. The gameplay combines shared resources, a day-night cycle, Martian dust storms and solar flares, and an on-screen bar of space habitat facts.

Design considerations: Controls work with a keyboard and mouse, and the game shows clear warnings before problems arrive. We simplified gravity, day length and radiation values so players focus on decisions. The current version uses no real NASA 3D models or textures.
